claims.text: Specific HfTi and TiZr short-range-order clusters form and percolate into B2-like ordered domains in HfNbTaTiZr.
Percolative B2-like ordering reduces local lattice-distortion amplitude relative to the random solid solution.
Reduced lattice distortion shifts the high-frequency phonon DOS to higher frequencies.
The DOS shift associated with ordering increases phonon group velocity.
Chemical ordering produces a net increase in lattice thermal conductivity relative to the random state.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr random solid solution has significant local lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch.
Thermal annealing or Monte Carlo equilibration can induce chemical short-range order.
The induced HfTi and TiZr clusters evolve into percolative B2-like structures.
Temperatures below the order-disorder transition but above a glass transition permit cluster formation and percolation without bulk phase separation.
An atomic-size-difference parameter of δ ≤ 6.6% is an appropriate boundary for maintaining single-phase stability in this system.
A percolative network of ordered binary clusters locally homogenizes the chemical environment.
Local chemical homogenization reduces the variance in force constants and lattice strain relative to a random distribution.
Transition from random to ordered binary regions reduces RMS lattice distortion and force-constant disorder.
Stiffer bonds in ordered regions shift the high-frequency phonon DOS to higher energies and reduce high-frequency phonon scattering phase space.
Percolated ordered clusters create continuous phonon-transport pathways that increase phonon mean free paths.
The ordered state should exhibit higher lattice thermal conductivity, an upshift of high-frequency DOS peaks, and lower pair-specific Debye-Waller factors than the random state.
Random HfNbTaTiZr has low thermal conductivity because random atomic-size and mass disorder strongly scatter phonons.
Below the SRO-cluster percolation threshold, isolated clusters do not produce the proposed conductivity increase.
Macroscopic phase separation or precipitate formation decreases conductivity through interface scattering.
Ordered-disordered interfaces can introduce additional phonon modes that counteract the conductivity gain by increasing scattering.
